stories.topic: How Ajay got hooked: Corbett, Everest books and the IIT Bombay mountaineering club
stories.summary: Ajay grew up on Jim Corbett's books and accounts of the first ascent of Everest, and has gone into the mountains since age 13. At IIT Bombay in the early 80s he joined a community that already existed. A physics professor, Professor Mahajan, had led the building of a mountaineering and rock-climbing culture there in the late 70s and early 80s. Gear was scarce and expensive, so the club pooled it. Members passed down how to run an overnight trek, a week-long trek, or a two-week trek in the Himalayas. Today the same knowledge comes from the internet and GPS, and good, cheap gear is easy to buy.
stories.insight: Lifelong passions are often seeded by childhood reading and kept alive by a community that hands down know-how you can't easily learn alone. Those barriers have mostly fallen. The main thing left is to not quit, as most people do in their teens and twenties.
stories.quote: I've been going out into the mountains from age 13 and I've just consistently gone back. So this has just been part of my life and I've taken it seriously as something that one should do and many people kind of give up in their teens and twenties, but I just kept going.

stories.topic: Goechala: the night that was too cold to sleep, and the decision to turn back
stories.summary: On the Goechala trek, the Sikkim-side approach to Kanchenjunga, Ajay slept in a one-person tent at the last campsite, Lamuney, at roughly 4,500-4,800 metres. The wind came up. Even in merino inners, fleece, a full-sleeve shirt and a jacket, inside a sleeping bag, he was kept awake all night by the cold. Wind chill, he explains, makes felt cold depend on wind speed, not just the thermometer. At 4 a.m. they started walking in ghostly moonlight, with so little oxygen that he took two or three breaths for every step. Other trekkers had given up after days of bad weather. His group got a clear day and reached Goechala 1, with Kanchenjunga in front of them. His guide said he could make Goechala 2, though not Goechala 3. Ajay said no: his gloves were bad, it was perhaps minus 10 or minus 20, and his fingertips hurt too much. He still wishes he had gone on.
stories.insight: The hardest call in the mountains is when to stop. A reason that feels 'stupid', like aching fingers, may have been early frostbite. You rarely know in the moment, and turning back with lifelong regret beats pressing on into damage.
stories.quote: All I know is that at that moment I desperately wanted to go, but I made the call that I can't handle this, I'm going back.

stories.topic: Porter on the first IIT Bombay climb of Konkan Kada
stories.summary: In his third year at IIT Bombay, Ajay was a 'coolie' on the first successful climb of Konkan Kada from IIT Bombay. Konkan Kada is the cobra-shaped overhanging west face of Harishchandragad, looking down into the Konkan almost to the sea. He made two long ferries up and down the face carrying 20 kg of food, water and climbing stores tied to his hip. On the last day he was the first person out. He rappelled about 1,800 feet through sheer overhang, and at each stop the rope's natural twist spun him 360 degrees while he took photographs all around.
stories.insight: You don't have to be the star climber to be part of something historic. Carrying loads for someone else's ambitious project can give you one of the great experiences of your life.
stories.quote: I have not done much technical climbing myself. I was a coolie. I was just a user of other people's rope systems.

stories.topic: Edward Weston and the rise and fall of pedestrianism
stories.summary: Amit retells the story from Matthew Algeo's book. In 1860 Edward Weston bet a friend that Lincoln would lose. If Lincoln won, Weston would walk from the State House in Boston to the Capitol in Washington in ten days. Lincoln won. Weston walked, took a little longer, and missed the inauguration, but the whole country followed his progress, much as it later followed Lindbergh. Weston decided walking should be a competitive sport. For about twenty years 'pedestrianism' was America's biggest spectator sport. Crowds paid to watch men circle tracks for six days a week, Sundays excepted. Weston, in hunting boots and breeches, was its Federer. The Irish working-man Dan O'Leary was its Nadal. The African American Frank Hart, O'Leary's protege known as 'Black Dan', was a third pillar. Early on, fans analysed technique: Weston's long strides against O'Leary's shorter, lighter steps. Later it became an ugly contest of who could stay awake for six days.
stories.insight: An activity done for love can turn competitive, then a spectacle, then toxic. Amit imagines the old champions, once the sport died, going out to walk alone again and rediscovering why they loved it.
stories.quote: But later on those techniques don't matter because it becomes a battle of staying awake. They are fighting sleep. For those six days they do not sleep.

stories.summary: Petrosian, the great grandmaster and pioneer of the exchange sacrifice, went partly deaf. Once, in a losing position, a young opponent who revered him offered a draw. Petrosian didn't hear it and went on to lose. In the main story, an opponent who badly wanted a draw tested the waters. He asked, 'Are you playing to win?' Petrosian said no. 'Are you playing to draw?' No. 'Then why are you playing?' Petrosian answered: 'I'm playing to play.'
stories.insight: The purest stance toward any pursuit is to do it for itself, not for the result or anyone's approval: hiking to hike, walking to walk. Amit offers it as a philosophy for life.
stories.quote: And Petrosian says I'm playing to play. I love this. This should be everybody's philosophy for life, that it is not about the win, it is not about the result.

stories.topic: How Ajay broke his ankle coming down from Tung
stories.summary: In the Sahyadris, Ajay's group did two up-and-down climbs in one day, the second being Tung, about a thousand metres up and five hundred down in all. From the top they could see the lake where they would camp. Back at the base there was a chai shop. Thinking the day was basically over, they had a fresh lime soda while the sun went down. He hadn't checked Google Earth, so he didn't realise there were still about 300 metres of descent to the lake. The view from the top had flattened the terrain. They set off late in failing light, got a little lost, and followed a pipe down toward the lake. A pipe takes the shortest, and so the steepest, line. Then came the bit of bad luck: he fell and broke his ankle. It was his first accident in 45 years of hiking.
stories.insight: The fall itself was bad luck, but the conditions for it were his own doing: no homework and a relaxed guard just when the day felt finished. Amit links it to Tom Vanderbilt's finding that most road accidents happen close to home, and to writing projects whose last stretch looks flat from above.
stories.quote: So my notes to self are that do a little more homework, understand every day what is the project that we are going to do... Never relax until the tent is up.

stories.topic: Outpaced by nobody: the Bangalore teenagers at Panchachuli
stories.summary: Ajay and his friend KP Krishnan went hiking to Panchachuli, near the India-China border in Uttarakhand, with a band of teenage boys and girls from Bangalore. The two older men assumed they would be the weakest link. Instead they were among the strongest. The teenagers, used to video games and Netflix, were strikingly unfit.
stories.insight: Youth no longer guarantees fitness. Ajay notes elsewhere that our grandparents had strength from agricultural work. Today, fitness is a habit you build, not something that comes with your age.
stories.quote: So it is really a new revelation for me. The idea that you can be young and not physically active.

recommendations.creator: Jim Corbett
recommendations.context: Ajay grew up on Corbett's books and names this first in his recommendations segment.
recommendations.reason: Part of the reading that made mountains and forests seem like 'the greatest thing in the world' to him. He calls Corbett's three best books 'really wonderful' and says everybody will enjoy them.

recommendations.creator: Jim Corbett
recommendations.context: The second of the three Corbett books Ajay suggests reading in sequence.
recommendations.reason: One of the three Corbett books he considers great.

recommendations.creator: Jim Corbett
recommendations.context: The third of the Corbett books Ajay singles out.
recommendations.reason: Completes his recommended Corbett sequence.

recommendations.creator: Jon Krakauer
recommendations.context: Raised right after the Goechala story, in the discussion of knowing when to stop. Ajay says it is a great book he would recommend to everybody.
recommendations.reason: It is about one summer on Everest when many bad things happened, and it shows the go/no-go call on the final summit day. Ajay says every Everest accident comes down to that judgment.

recommendations.creator: Jon Krakauer
recommendations.context: Added alongside Into Thin Air in the recommendations segment.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says Krakauer has 'some really good books' and this is another one.

recommendations.creator: Ernest Hemingway
recommendations.context: Ajay's thought experiment on why mountains and forests matter.
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the great books of the world. Move its story to a purely urban setting and 'the oomph is lost', which shows how much wild landscapes add to a story and to life.

recommendations.creator: Edward O. Wilson
recommendations.context: Ajay cites Wilson's term when Amit asks if his love of hiking is part of a turn toward nature.
recommendations.reason: 'Biophilia', a perception of and presence with all forms of nature, names what Ajay feels hiking gives him.

recommendations.item: Prem Throws Your Heart to the Ground
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's newsletter post from the day before recording, which quotes Dilip Chitre's poem.
recommendations.reason: It leads into his question of whether urban, thing-filled living estranges us from something essential.

recommendations.creator: Dilip Chitre
recommendations.context: Quoted in Amit's newsletter post. He calls it a great poem.
recommendations.reason: Its phrase 'man's estrangement from a man-made world' stuck with him, and he uses it to ask whether embracing nature makes you a different person.

recommendations.item: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
recommendations.creator: Robert M. Pirsig
recommendations.context: Ajay quotes it while explaining why he hikes.
recommendations.reason: Its line 'the Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there' captures his point: what you get from the mountains depends on the mind you bring.

recommendations.creator: Matthew Algeo
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a great book and retells its story of Edward Weston and the six-day walking matches.
recommendations.reason: It is a vivid case of a pastime loved for itself being turned into a competitive spectacle and turning ugly.

recommendations.creator: Tom Vanderbilt
recommendations.context: Raised after Ajay's ankle story. Amit calls it a great book.
recommendations.reason: His takeaway: most accidents happen close to home, because familiar ground makes the brain switch off. That is exactly what happened to Ajay below Tung.

recommendations.creator: Adam Gopnik
recommendations.context: A New Yorker essay on walking that Amit came across recently. It covers pedestrianism at length.
recommendations.reason: Amit enjoys its lines ('our backs and arches, like querulous cabinet ministers, at first complain and then resign'). He also likes its argument that walking as a pastime depended on technologies such as gaslight, the rule of law, the Walkman and sneakers.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Ajay criticises sitting around eating processed food. Amit calls it a great episode on nutrition and diabetes.
recommendations.reason: It is background for why processed food is to be avoided. That matters on the trail too, where Ajay found from a CGM that Maggi noodles and maida still spike you.

recommendations.context: Ajay's answer when Amit asks where to buy hiking gear in India.
recommendations.reason: After a lifetime of hunting for the right equipment, he calls Decathlon's arrival a breakthrough: good gear, readily available and affordable.

recommendations.item: A 75-litre backpack (Ajay uses the Volt 75), and a women's-fit pack for women
recommendations.context: Kit discussion for multi-day hikes.
recommendations.reason: Any old backpack works for a day hike. For big trips, 75 litres fits a sleeping bag and clothes, and he says people often buy too small or too big. He strongly encourages women to hike, for the freedom and resilience it builds, and notes women's backpacks are cut differently.

recommendations.creator: LifeStraw
recommendations.context: Water-filter recommendations.
recommendations.reason: You can fill it with any bad water, and sucking pushes it through a filter. Ajay says the output is cleaner than any tap water in India.

recommendations.creator: Katadyn
recommendations.context: The filter Ajay says he has taken on all his hikes.
recommendations.reason: You fill a six-litre bag and gravity pushes the water through a filter. He calls it a big gain that many Indian hikers are not yet using.

recommendations.creator: Indiahikes
recommendations.context: Amit asks for a resource for researching hikes.
recommendations.reason: Ajay has never used them as a services firm, but for almost any hike in India their page is often the best, with the story, the route and a map. From there you can move to Google Earth.

recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: The main lesson from his ankle injury, and his research tool for every trek.
recommendations.reason: Check the elevation of the summit, the base of the climb and your campsite before you go, so you know the whole day's work. He says the desktop version beats the browser one.

recommendations.context: A Bombay hiking services firm.
recommendations.reason: Ajay has gone with them on many of his trips and likes their work a lot.

recommendations.context: A Delhi hiking services firm.
recommendations.reason: It runs a fixed calendar of treks, so you can show up alone and join others without organising your own group.

recommendations.context: Named as phenomenal, accessible day hikes in the Bombay/Maharashtra region.
recommendations.reason: They are an easy first step: a backpack, two litres of water, five apples and some route-finding. Enough people use them that you'll meet someone to set you right.

recommendations.context: Ajay calls this Western Sahyadris region one of the most memorable places in the world.
recommendations.reason: He calls it world class and says he has never seen anything more beautiful. He also warns it is now overrun by boorish young men with alcohol.

recommendations.context: The Sikkim-side approach to Kanchenjunga.
recommendations.reason: Of all his Himalayan treks, he rates it one of the best of his life. Reaching Goechala 1 with Kanchenjunga in front of him was one of his life's great moments.

core_ideas.concept: We are monkeys: city life leaves a hole
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay extends Marx's idea of alienation beyond the assembly-line worker. Biologically we are one more branch of the tree of life, built to live among trees. A life spent among concrete, coffee shops and bars leaves something missing. Amit frames the same idea with Dilip Chitre's phrase 'man's estrangement from a man-made world'.
core_ideas.quote: As every good biologist will say to you, we are not like monkeys. We are monkeys.

core_ideas.concept: Marx: right on the diagnosis, wrong on the cure
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay credits Marx with being first to see how capitalism, globalisation and the market economy act like a 'wild west wind' that tears down feudalism and old social customs and brings modernity. He says Marx was wrong on essentially every remedy. Amit adds that getting the description right and the prescription wrong is practically a feature of leftist thought.
core_ideas.quote: He was right on a lot of his understanding of the world. He was wrong on essentially everything he proposed on how to fix the world.

core_ideas.concept: The principle of the greatest problem
core_ideas.explanation: On a long climb, the body always complains about whatever is scarcest at that point. When oxygen is plentiful, your thighs complain. When your legs are strong, your lungs do. The constraint you must fight keeps moving, so you focus on whichever one binds now.
core_ideas.quote: If you have plenty of oxygen, your body will whine that your thighs are unhappy. If you have ample strength in your legs, your body will whine that I don't have enough oxygen.

core_ideas.concept: Know when to stop: no sunk costs, no performance
core_ideas.explanation: Above roughly 7,500 metres, the 'dead zone', you are beyond the design spec of the human body, and your judgment degrades along with everything else. Ajay says every Everest accident comes down to the go/turn-back call. Years of training (sunk cost) and wanting to post the summit photo both push people to continue. Amit adds that, as with drinking, judgment fails just when you need it, and risk-takers start out biased toward going on.
core_ideas.quote: We should be cold, we should not suffer from sunk cost fallacy. Life is not lived as a performance to show other people. We should do things for the human being inside us.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's summary of the pedestrianism story. Great ideas start as something done for love, get monetised, and end as a racket. He applies it to rock climbing, which he sees as a solitary puzzle like a crossword, now turned into speed competitions, and to people who climb mountains to brag on social media. The antidote is Petrosian's 'playing to play': keep the activity free of competition and performance.
core_ideas.quote: It is the fate of every great idea to start out as a movement and then become a business and then become a racket.

core_ideas.concept: The demand is in the mind: hiking as moving meditation
core_ideas.explanation: A day of hiking can burn two to four thousand calories, but it is spread over hours of gentle slopes in 30-60 minute stints with breaks. If you can row or run for 10-20 minutes, your body is ready. The real challenge is mental: settling into a meditative zone where you watch your breathing, heart and calves. People fill the zone differently. KP Krishnan recites thousands of Sanskrit shlokas as he walks. Short bursts of speed followed by panting don't work.
core_ideas.quote: So it's not like the fitness demands are out of this world. The demand is in the mind, meaning it's about the mind being able to handle the body.

core_ideas.concept: Don't go casually: modest fitness, basic kit, real preparation
core_ideas.explanation: On easy tourist routes like Triund behind Dharamshala, and on pilgrimages like Gangotri, Ajay sees people suffering because they arrive unfit, in party clothes, after watching miraculous YouTube clips. Their grandparents had farm-work strength. People who sit watching Netflix and eating processed food don't. Basic fitness, proper footwear, some kit and mental preparation turn the trip from torture into joy. Separately, real danger begins with technical climbing: if you're not using your hands, trekking itself is not truly dangerous.
core_ideas.quote: But in today's world, if you're sitting on your butt watching Netflix and eating processed food, you're not ready.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's path for beginners. Start with day hikes, ideally with people who know the route. If you find yourself at a summit wishing you didn't have to go back, pitch a tent: one night, then two, seven, ten. In India today, tents beat the caves and temples people once slept in. Long routes mean learning to live off the land by buying food in villages. Once you can do that, there's no natural stopping point. On a north-south route in Maharashtra, he and Ayush Patnaik have looked at each other around day seven and realised they could just walk on to Kanyakumari.
core_ideas.quote: So once you get going, it's really unstoppable and you don't feel like stopping. You don't feel like coming back. You can just keep on going forever.

core_ideas.concept: Leave no trace, respect the silence
core_ideas.explanation: There is no one to clean up the mountains, so don't litter and bring your plastic back. Wet wipes made with nylon or polyester are plastic and pollute for a thousand years, so buy all-cotton, biodegradable ones. Bluetooth speakers and loud talk carry for hundreds of metres in mountain silence and spoil the experience for everyone. Speak in whispers and you will see more birds and wildlife.
core_ideas.quote: So if you go to the mountains, please engage in hushed whispers because your entire experience will change. You will experience nature better.

core_ideas.concept: Treat the mountain crew as teammates, not hotel staff
core_ideas.explanation: India's elite are used to demanding service from hotels. In the mountains the crew is carrying your load, cooking and washing dishes at altitude, and their means are limited. Ask for things, take no for an answer with a smile (black coffee when the creamer runs out), and do your own small tasks. Amit notes this is good advice for everyday life too, since we only need it because we behave badly at home.
core_ideas.quote: Treat them like teammates, don't treat them like your employees.

core_ideas.concept: Character is how you behave under stress
core_ideas.explanation: On real adventures, especially in the Sahyadris, which are less 'corseted' than standard Himalayan routes, you will run short of water, get lost, or have someone fall ill. Arul Menezes once got kidney stones at the top of Harishchandragad. These setbacks become good stories later. What matters is staying calm, solving problems, and not taking it out on others.
core_ideas.quote: So you know my dharma always is that the bigger the crisis, the calmer and more thoughtful I become.

core_ideas.concept: Never relax until the tent is up
core_ideas.explanation: The lesson of Ajay's broken ankle. Danger peaks when you think the job is done. Do your homework (Google Earth elevations of summit, base and campsite), stay fully present until the end of the day, and avoid shortcuts like following pipes, which take the steepest line. Amit connects it to Tom Vanderbilt's finding that accidents cluster near home, and to writing: from high up, the last stretch always looks flat.
core_ideas.quote: You can never let your guard down. You know, you have to think, you have to be there with full presence and energy.

core_ideas.concept: Eat carefully on the trail, especially at dinner
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay assumed burning thousands of calories gave him licence to eat anything. Hiking with a CGM showed him that Maggi, white rice and maida still spike your blood sugar. Dinner matters most because you burn almost nothing afterwards. Include some protein, such as dal and eggs, and look for micronutrients, since trail food is all cooked.
core_ideas.quote: Most notably we have to be careful around dinner time, because after dinner you're not burning.

core_ideas.concept: Walking as a pastime depends on technology
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Adam Gopnik's essay, Amit argues that walking for pleasure was never simply natural. Gaslight let Londoners walk after dark. The rule of law made streets safe, especially for women. From the 1980s, the Walkman and cushioned sneakers made walking easier still. Each layer removes drudgery so we can attend to the experience itself.
core_ideas.quote: It is something that is far easier for us to do in modern times and to take the drudgery out of it by using all these different technologies.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged that that which we love the most hurts us the most. And today you will see my fellow cast member in a cast.' Then, on Ajay saying the worst is behind him: 'though at that time I was standing behind you.'

Amit on Ajay's message mid-hike: Ajay had said 'Amit, you won't hear from me for a week', and 'in the middle of that blissful period of mental peace and calm' came the news that he'd broken his ankle. Amit also calls him a hiking evangelist, meaning 'a person who evangelises hiking and not that while hiking you evangelise.'

Amit, looking at each camera in turn, warns viewers that Ajay's 'great German philosopher' (Marx) and 'the good Lord intended' are ironic: 'we are not actually fans of Marx... at least I am certain there is no good lord. However, monkeys do exist and we are monkeys.'
On the background music from a festival two villages away: 'This is not green screen, though it is green... This is also a part of nature. Humans are monkeys.'

Ajay's call to action: 'We said to gentle reader, get off your butt and read some books. Today we're saying, gentle reader, get off your butt and go take a hike.' Amit hopes listeners are getting up to walk 'not because they're sick of the show.'
After Ajay says you should be able to 'row or run' for 20 minutes, Amit clarifies: 'by row we mean the English row', a bilingual pun on the Hindi for crying.
Told hikers should carry 5-15% of body weight, Amit says: 'This is why, Ajay, you should be overweight like me, because then you're carrying a lower percentage.' Ajay: 'I don't recommend it.'
Amit, stung by the Netflix jibe: 'My question for you is on whose butt should I sit. I'll sit on my butt only, no?'
Ajay explains the zo, a yak-cow cross with 'the strength of the yak and the domesticity of a cow'. Amit: 'Jimi Hendrix has a song called Hazo. I wonder whether he was thinking of it.'
After Ajay recalls Arul Menezes howling with kidney stones atop Harishchandragad, Amit asks: 'Have you asked Arul before sharing this anecdote?'
Amit on turning mishaps into stories: 'That is how YouTubers think of content. So what if I broke my ankle? Content mila.'

Ajay calls Google Earth 'the greatest joy in the world'. Amit: 'Google Earth is not the greatest joy on earth. It's bacon.' He later closes the lesson: 'even after you do switch off, don't eat too much for dinner.'
On the five apples for a day hike, Amit: 'And by apples you mean the fruit, not iPad and MacBook.'
Ajay's 'funny correlation': lots of physics people go hiking, because you experience gravity, light and air at a different level altogether.
Green Boots: Amit mentions the famous photograph of one of the bodies preserved on Everest, which led him to ask why people climb at all.

Amit casts the pedestrianism greats as tennis greats: Weston as Federer, Dan O'Leary as Nadal, and Frank 'Black Dan' Hart as a possible Djokovic. He likens the national frenzy over Weston's walk to Lindbergh's a few decades later.
Amit on France, home of Decathlon, as a great outdoor-sports culture and a centre of ultra-running, home to the UTMB (Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc).
Ajay's closing self-portrait: 'if I had not been an economist, I would be a biologist.'
